title: Lucky to bear it
hookLine: not "I'm unlucky," but "I'm lucky to bear this without breaking" (Meditations 4.49)
last: SPRAY FLIES UP AND FALLS BACK.

cards: Listen to how people tell bad news. Just my luck. Why does this always happen to me?
The sentence starts before we've decided what we think: a little reflex story about being the unlucky one.
In the same entry as the headland, a few lines later, Marcus Aurelius catches himself in exactly that reflex, and rewrites the sentence. Same event. Different words.
And the new words change what the event is.

teach.b: Unlucky me, that this happened, Marcus imagines saying. Then he corrects himself. Not at all.
Rather: lucky me, that though this happened, I'm still standing, not crushed by the present and not afraid of what's coming. Why call that luck?

teach.h: ANYONE COULD MEET IT; NOT ALL BEAR IT.
teach.b: Something like this could have happened to anyone, he says, but not everyone would have come through it unbroken. So why call the event bad luck, rather than calling your steadiness good luck?
Both are true; you choose the headline. Then a test.

teach.h: DOES IT STOP YOU BEING JUST?
teach.b: Does what happened stop you from being just, generous, self-controlled, sensible, careful in judgment, honest, modest, free? If it doesn't touch those, it hasn't touched what makes you who you are.

teach.h: BEARING IT WELL IS GOOD FORTUNE.
teach.b: And a rule for every future vexation: this is not a misfortune, but bearing it well is good fortune. This isn't pretending. Marcus doesn't call the loss a gain, or say it didn't hurt.
He moves the word luck from the event, which you didn't choose, to the bearing, which is yours. The flat tire is a flat tire.
Changing it calmly, on the shoulder, in the rain, without taking it out on anyone: that's the part that's yours, and it's a kind of luck to be able to.

how: Readers of Marcus Aurelius often apply the rule at the end of Meditations 4.49 to setbacks: the event is not a misfortune, but bearing it well is good fortune.

o: luck found in bearing a hard thing well
a lucky break that comes out of nowhere
an event that turns out well by chance

games.q: your flight is canceled and you'll miss a friend's party. what fits Meditations 4.49?

games.why: Marcus doesn't call the loss good. he says this isn't misfortune; bearing it well is good fortune.

practice: Bring to mind one misfortune, recent or old, and hear the reflex sentence first: just my luck. Then try Marcus's rewrite, this happened and I'm still standing, and ask his test: did it stop me from being fair, honest, kind?
If not, say quietly: lucky to bear it.

wordCard.voice: Good fortune. Marcus moves luck from the event to the bearing: this isn't misfortune, but to bear it well is good fortune. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, 'fortunate, lucky': Marcus's rewrite in 4.49 turns 'unlucky me' into this word.

carryVoice: Your line: still standing, not crushed. Luck lives in the bearing, not the event. That's day five hundred sixty-one.
